key_messages: Dry weather with seasonable temperatures will continue through Friday, with areas of frost expected again tonight.
Latest forecast shows increasing probability of a wetting rainfall this weekend for portions of VT, along with localized areas of cooler temperatures and breezy winds associated with coastal system.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
224 PM EDT Wed Sep 23 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 223 PM EDT Wednesday...

Frost Advisories have been issued in the northern St. Lawrence 
Valley, the Champlain Valley, outside of Grand Isle County in 
Vermont, and portions of central and southern Vermont from 2 AM to 9 
AM Thursday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 223 PM EDT Wednesday...

1. Dry weather with seasonable temperatures will continue 
through Friday, with areas of frost expected again tonight. 

2. Latest forecast shows increasing probability of a wetting 
rainfall this weekend for portions of VT, along with localized areas 
of cooler temperatures and breezy winds associated with coastal 
system. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 223 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure remains centered just to our north this 
afternoon, keeping conditions calm, dry and cool. There is a 
noticeable lack of fair weather cumulus clouds as compared to 
yesterday, due to significant drying in the low to mid levels. PWats 
across the area are dropping to 0.2-0.4 inches, resulting in 
dewpoints in the upper 30s for most of the area. These lower 
dewpoints will set up our cooling potential tonight with another 
round of clear skies and strong radiational cooling expected. 
Temperatures will dip below 40 degrees for majority of the area 
again tonight, even into portions of southern Vermont where mid to 
upper 30s can be expected. Widespread near freezing temperatures 
will be possible across the Northeast Kingdom, central Vermont 
valleys, and the Adirondacks. Pocket mid to upper 20s will be likely 
in isolated portions of the northern Adirondacks. Frost Advisories 
have been issued for the northern St. Lawrence Valley, the Champlain 
Valley outside of Grand Isle County in Vermont, and portions of 
central and southern Vermont from 2 AM to 9 AM Thursday. Frost will 
be less likely near and long Lake Champlain, generally within 5 
miles of the lake, due to the surrounding warmer water temperatures 
helping to moderate the surrounding air. Furthermore, areas in lower 
valleys will have the better chance for any frost, with areas in 
higher terrain less likely to experience frost. Patchy fog will once 
again be possible in the climo favored river valleys of Vermont and 
northern New York, though the onset and spatial coverage may be less 
than last night due to lower crossover temperatures, and slightly 
less moisture.

Through the late week, temperatures will slowly creep up a degree or 
two each day towards Friday, with highs in the mid to upper 60s, as 
the high drifts to the northeast. Clouds begin to build Thursday 
into Friday as a nor'easter off the southern New England Coast 
meanders close to the coast. There is still a large degree of 
uncertainty with regards to the evolution of the system, as it 
pertains to cloud cover and precipitation chances. Currently it 
looks like Friday should remain dry for now with PoPs well below 
30%. A tightening pressure gradient by Friday will develop across 
our area resulting in some breezy channeled winds potentially Friday 
afternoon into Saturday. Model soundings support gusts potentially 
between 25-35 MPH in the Champlain Valley by Saturday afternoon. The 
higher terrain of the eastern Greens and Adirondacks will also see 
these gusty winds Saturday along with temperatures in the upper 40s. 
Those interested in viewing any fall colors in the mountains of 
northern New York and or Vermont should prepare for breezy and 
seasonably cold conditions. Temperatures in generally will be cool 
on Saturday with highs in the valleys only in the low to mid 60s 
with increased cloud cover and cool advective easterly winds.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Latest trends in the 12z guidance continues to 
retrograde deeply closed cyclonic circulation closer to the southern 
New England Coast this weekend and bring higher probabilities of 
measurable precipitation into portions of VT. In addition, localized 
breezy winds acrs the higher terrain and the Champlain Valley is 
increasing, along with cooler than average temps. This event 
continues to be challenge with a low predictability on exact 
impacts/details at this stage of the game. 

The 13Z NBM and 00Z LREF data shows 10% prob of QPF>0.10" at MSS, 
near 40% at BTV and 70% at VSF, while prob of QPF>0.25" is 5% at 
MSS, 30% at BTV and 60% at VSF. Interesting to note, is the 
continued large spread in potential QPF output by latest guidance, 
which shows the 25th percentile of 0.00" and 75th of 1.06" at VSF 
and 0.00 to 0.53" at MPV and 0.00 to 0.27" at BTV. Given the above 
scenario, the pops from WPC wl show a sharp nw to se gradient acrs 
our cwa this aftn, along with the associated qpf output. Similar to 
a winter type event, any further shift east or west in the progged 
sfc low pres track wl have an influence on pops/qpf acrs our cwa 
this upcoming weekend. Highest pops wl be Sat night into Sunday acrs 
our southern and eastern cwa per latest WPC forecast. Still feel as 
bands of deeper moisture and QPF advect from east to west acrs our 
cwa this weekend and encounters deep dry layer, precip intensity wl 
weaken, especially acrs the CPV and northern Dacks. 

In addition, have noted increasing 925-850mb wind fields of 30 to 45 
knots acrs our cwa, along with inversion height near summit level, 
helping to enhance winds toward the sfc. Expecting localized gusts 
acrs the mtns of VT in the 25 to 35 mph range, with similar values 
over Lake Champlain. If current trends hold with track of sfc low 
pres, a prolonged Lake Wind Advisory wl likely be needed from 
Saturday night thru Sunday night. As probability of clouds/precip 
increases, especially for central/eastern VT and associated trrn, 
the potential for cooler temps on Sunday is increasing too. Highs 
could struggle in the mid/upper 40s east/central mtns to near 70 
SLV. 

By early next week coastal system lifts northeast and mid/upper lvl 
ridge builds into the Mid Atlantic/NE CONUS. This wl result in drier 
air with above normal temps returns by the start of the new work 
week. Highs mid 60s to lower 70s with lows upper 30s to lower 50s, 
could even be warmer by Tues/Weds next week.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 18Z Thursday...Aviation challenge is timing and areal
coverage of fog and associated IFR or lower conditions.
Currently VFR conditions prevail at all taf sites, but did not
sfc dewpoints are 3 to 5 degrees lower this aftn, which will
delay development of fog as it takes a bit longer to reach cross
over values. Given the fog development last night and latest
sounding data feel the highest probability of fog (80-90%) will
be at EFK/MPV and SLK between 08z-13z. Similar to last night 
brief IFR is possible at MSS near sunrise on Thurs, and some
Winooski River Valley fog could impact the north end of the
runaway at BTV near sunrise. Otherwise northwest to northeast
winds 4 to 8 knots become light east/southeast tonight, before
shifting to the north again on Thursday. 

Outlook...

Friday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
